title: A Bus Ride to Fight for Voting Rights, Just Like 60 Years Ago
summary: Imagine getting on a bus not for a field trip, but to fight for your right to vote. That's what dozens of people did on Saturday, May 16, 2026. They traveled from Atlanta, Georgia, to Montgomery, Alabama—the same city where, in 1965, brave marchers were beaten while demanding voting rights for Black Americans. This time, the bus riders were protesting a new Supreme Court ruling. The court said it's wrong to consider race when drawing voting maps. Because of that, states like Alabama redrew their districts in ways that make it harder for Black voters to elect leaders who represent them. Keith Odom, a 62-year-old forklift driver and grandfather, was one of the riders. "I want to go forward, for my grandchildren to be able to go forward," he said. The youngest protester was 18-year-old Kobe Chernushin, who filmed the event for social media. The buses left from a district once represented by John Lewis, a famous civil rights leader who was beaten in 1965. Today, a bill named after him could protect voting rights again. But for now, the fight continues.
why_it_matters: Who draws voting maps can affect who makes rules about your school, parks, and community, so the fight for fair voting touches your life too.

background_read: In 1965, brave marchers including John Lewis (a young civil rights activist at the time) tried to walk from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, to demand equal voting rights.
On a day called 'Bloody Sunday,' police attacked the marchers, but their courage led to the Voting Rights Act, which helped protect Black voters.
Even today, the Supreme Court (the top U.S. court) makes decisions that change how voting maps are drawn, stirring new debates about fairness.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dozens of protesters, including 62-year-old Keith Odom and 18-year-old Kobe Chernushin
WHAT: A bus ride from Atlanta to Montgomery to protest a Supreme Court ruling on voting maps
WHERE: From Atlanta, Georgia, to Montgomery, Alabama – a route tied to civil rights history
WHY: The court’s ruling made it harder for Black voters to elect candidates who represent them, so protesters want to keep the fight for fair voting alive

perspectives.description: Protesters believe their ride honors the past and pushes the country to treat all voters equally, just like marchers in 1965 dreamed.
Some people think the Supreme Court’s ruling was right because race should not be the main factor when drawing maps, and they worry about other ways of grouping voters.
The story shows that questions about fairness in voting never fully end – each generation must decide how to draw lines that make elections truly equal.
